content: Start by reading TASK.md, then complete the assignment.

content.content:
1	# Task 11: Solar-system explorer with focus on click
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The app is an interactive, stylised solar system explorer on a dark starfield background.
4	
5	Show a glowing central star and at least 6 planets, each at a different orbital distance, with a different size and colour and orbiting the star at a different speed (inner planets faster). At least one planet has a moon orbiting it, and at least one planet has a ring. Draw a thin circular orbit line for each planet. Planets should also spin about their own axis. Use a simple procedural look (colour, gradients or generated textures); do not load external assets from the network.
6	
7	The user can click a planet to focus on it. On focus, the camera smoothly moves (about 1.5 seconds, eased) to a close view of that planet and keeps following it as it orbits, and a DOM info panel appears showing the planet's name, its orbital period in Earth days, and its distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space, or pressing the Escape key, smoothly returns to the overview showing the whole system and hides the panel. In the overview, the user can drag to orbit the camera around the system and scroll to zoom within sensible limits. Add a toggle button labelled 'Pause' that stops and resumes orbital motion, and shows 'Play' while paused.
8	
9	The scene must look correct on first load with no console errors. Expose

content.thinking:
I'm planning the layout with DOM UI elements positioned over a 640x360 canvas, and mapping out the solar system bodies—Mercury through Uranus, including Earth's moon and Saturn's ring—with scaled orbit radii and realistic day periods.

For orbital speed, I'll use a non-linear scaling so faster inner planets don't look absurdly quick relative to outer ones, settling on a formula where period in seconds scales with (days/365.25)^0.7, giving Mercury ~11s and Uranus ~660s per orbit.

For camera focus, I'm designing a follow system where the camera offsets from the planet away from the star, lerping smoothly between overview and focused states, disabling OrbitControls while tracking a planet and restoring saved state on unfocus.

Now I'm working out click detection logic — distinguishing drags from clicks via pointer movement threshold, raycasting against planet hit-spheres, and handling focus/unfocus transitions including edge cases like clicking empty space or already being in overview. I'm also planning a sun glow effect using an additively-blended sprite with a radial gradient texture.

For materials, I'm giving the sun an emissive basic material with a central point light, planets get standard materials with procedural canvas textures (banded for gas giants, noisy for rocky ones), plus ambient lighting and a large starfield sphere. I'm calculating sizes and orbital radii for each planet, working out a good default overview camera position and field-of-view that fits the whole system in frame, and setting min/max zoom limits. I'm also laying out real distances in millions of kilometers for each planet to scale the orbits proportionally.

Now I'm working out orbital periods for each planet and structuring the group hierarchy: each planet sits on an orbit pivot positioned via sine/cosine, with the mesh itself spinning, and moons nested as child pivots. For Saturn's rings I'm building a radial gradient texture by remapping the ring geometry's UVs based on distance from center, using a striped alpha canvas with transparency and disabled depth writing. I'm finalizing planet radii and orbit spacing values.

For the focus camera, I'm computing distance based on planet radius (and Saturn's ring extent) and figuring out the offset direction so the camera sees the planet's lit side rather than its shadowed side relative to the star.

For the moon's orbit around Earth, I need the camera distance scaled appropriately. Pausing should stop all time-based updates including orbit and spin together for simplicity. For the read-only task state, I'll use Object.defineProperty with getters so the exposed window object stays frozen while planet data rebuilds fresh each frame.

For camera control during focus transitions, I'll disable OrbitControls while animating and just set position/target directly each frame via lerp and lookAt, only re-enabling controls.update() once the transition completes and I'm back in overview mode.

For lighting, I'm going with a PointLight at intensity 5 with decay 0 to account for the newer physically-based units, plus a subtle ambient light, and building the sun as a procedurally textured mesh with additive glow sprites layered on top for the corona effect.

Now I'm writing the planet texture generators (rocky blotches and gas bands via seeded canvas noise), orbit rings as transparent line loops, and setting up the renderer and UI panel/button positioning in the corners of the canvas.

I'm also adding an absolutely-positioned pointer-events wrapper over the canvas for UI elements, an escape key listener, and figuring out raycasting -- using invisible hit-sphere meshes so I can click planets reliably even though visibility doesn't affect raycast results, only render layers do.

For hit-testing I'll raycast against all hit spheres plus the Sun, take the first intersection, and only trigger focus if it's a planet's hit sphere (Sun clicks do nothing, moons ignored), storing names in userData for tooltips. I'm structuring each planet as a group hierarchy -- position group, then a tilt group for axial tilt, then the spinning mesh and ring -- with moons parented to the outer group, and using a seeded mulberry32 random function for texture generation.

I'm tracking simulation time that only accumulates when unpaused, computing each planet's angle from its phase plus elapsed time over its orbital period, clamping delta time, and using real (unpaused) time for a 1.5s eased camera transition between focus targets. I'm setting up Three.js imports with OrbitControls, giving planets distinct initial phases so they're spread around their orbits, remapping ring UVs based on radial distance for proper texture mapping, flattening the ring with a rotation, generating a radial gradient canvas for the sun's glow, and building a starfield of colored points on a large sphere with attenuation disabled.

Finally I'm tuning the camera's near/far clipping planes and writing a helper to compute distance from the camera to a focused planet's world position.

I'm checking the edge cases around transitions between focus and overview states, verifying that camera position, target, and controls update correctly during each phase. Everything looks consistent across focusing, unfocusing, and the overview end state.

content.text:
I wrote the solar-system explorer in `src/main.ts`. It passes `typecheck`, but I haven't built it with `vite build` or run it in a browser, so I haven't seen the rendered scene or tried the clicks.

- **Scene:** A glowing star sits on a starfield. Seven planets (Mercury to Uranus) orbit it, each at a different distance, size and colour. Inner planets move faster, and every planet spins and has a thin orbit line. Earth has a moon and Saturn has a ring. All textures are generated on canvases, so nothing is loaded from the network.
- **Focus:** Clicking a planet moves the camera to it over 1.5 seconds with easing, then it keeps following the planet. An info panel shows the name, orbital period in Earth days and distance from the star in million km. Clicking empty space or pressing Escape returns to the overview over 1.5 seconds and hides the panel.
- **Overview controls:** Dragging orbits the camera and scrolling zooms between 25 and 260 units. The Pause button toggles to "Play" while paused.
- **Pause scope:** Pause also freezes planet spin and the moon, not just the orbits.
- **Page hooks:** `window.__TASK_STATE__` is read-only and has the requested fields. `__focusPlanet(name)` and `__unfocus()` do the same as a click on that planet and a click on empty space. `__EVAL_READY__` is set after the first frame is drawn.
- **Orbital speeds:** They are compressed to fit on screen. Earth takes 30 seconds per orbit and Uranus about 11 minutes.

While touring the button reads 'Stop tour'; clicking it ends the tour and returns to the overview. Add touring: boolean to window.__TASK_STATE__.
Make this change in the existing project, check it with typecheck, then call finish again.

content.thinking:
I should keep the button outside the canvas overlay, placing it in normal document flow below the canvas instead of absolutely positioned over it. Now I'm sketching the tour logic, with a touring flag, index, and timer that advances every 3 seconds.

For user interactions during the tour, I want manual clicks, Escape, or stop-button presses to cancel it—but I need to separate the "cancel tour" state change from the actual unfocus action, so clicking a planet mid-tour transitions smoothly rather than unfocusing then refocusing abruptly.

I also need to handle edge cases: starting a tour while a planet is already focused (like Mercury) should just reset the timer since focusPlanet already exits early when the target matches the current focus, and orbit controls stay disabled appropriately during focused states.

I'm checking the ordering of declarations — making sure the tour section, state getters, and focusPlanet references all resolve correctly since they depend on each other being defined before use, and it looks consistent.

input.summary: I added a "Tour" button in a toolbar below the canvas, outside it, and `touring` on `window.__TASK_STATE__`. `typecheck` passes. I haven't built the app or run it in a browser, so the tour itself is untested. The tour focuses each planet in turn from Mercury to Uranus for 3 seconds each, including the 1.5 s camera move. The info panel shows during each stop, and the camera returns to the overview after Uranus. While the tour runs the button reads "Stop tour", and clicking it ends the tour and returns to the overview. A click on a planet or empty space, Escape, `__focusPlanet` and `__unfocus` also end the tour before doing their normal action. The 3-second tour timer uses real time, so it keeps running while the scene is paused.
